html:
The Fourche Maline culture was a Native American culture of the area where Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas and Louisiana meet, from about 800 BCE to 800 CE. It is named after Fourche Maline Creek in eastern Oklahoma.

People lived in villages along rivers. They hunted deer, fished, gathered nuts and grew squash and local seed plants of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Their sites are known for dark refuse heaps, called black middens, where they also buried some of their dead. They made thick pottery and traded with the Marksville culture and the wider Hopewell world.

They are seen as ancestors of the Caddo, whose chiefdoms grew up in the same region after about 800 CE and built mound centres such as Spiro, part of the Mississippian world.
